title: Concept Drills — Potential, Potential Difference & Potential Energy (Class 11 Physics)
subject: physics

questions.question: Why define electric potential (V = U/q) instead of working with potential energy directly?
questions.solution: Potential energy depends on BOTH the source and the test charge; dividing by q strips the test charge out and leaves a property of the SOURCE and the location alone. Potential is the energy landscape per coulomb — the same map works for any charge placed there, which is why circuits are described in volts.

questions.concept: Field points down the potential hill
questions.question: Why does E point from high to low potential, and what does E = −dV/dr encode?
questions.solution: Positive charges accelerate from high to low potential (losing PE, gaining KE), so the force — and E — points 'downhill'. E = −dV/dr says the field is the negative GRADIENT of potential: the steeper the potential change, the stronger the field; zero gradient means zero field even if V is large.

questions.question: Why is no work done moving a charge along an equipotential surface, and what does that imply about the field's direction there?
questions.solution: All points on the surface have the same V, so ΔV = 0 and W = qΔV = 0. Since W = qE·d·cosθ = 0 for nonzero displacement, E must be PERPENDICULAR to the surface — field lines cross equipotentials at right angles. The geometry of one determines the other.

questions.question: Why is the potential energy of two like charges positive and of unlike charges negative?
questions.solution: PE is the work needed to assemble the pair from infinite separation. Pushing two LIKE charges together against repulsion requires positive work — energy stored, U > 0. Unlike charges attract: they release energy as they come together, so U < 0 (energy must be ADDED to separate them). Sign records whether the pair is bound.

questions.question: Why do atomic physicists use the electron volt instead of the joule?
questions.solution: An electron crossing 1 V gains e×1 V = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J — an absurdly small number of joules for atomic-scale energies. The eV is a NATURAL unit for particle energies (1 eV, 13.6 eV, keV, MeV), making numbers human-sized. It is energy (charge × potential difference), not a voltage.

questions.concept: Why potential is a scalar while field is a vector
questions.question: Computing the field from several charges needs vector addition, but computing potential needs only simple addition of numbers. Why?
questions.solution: Potential is energy per unit charge — a SCALAR with a sign, so contributions add algebraically: V = Σkq/r. Field is a force per unit charge — a VECTOR, so contributions add with directions. Potential is easier to compute and to sum; the field is then recovered as E = −dV/dr. Scalars first, vectors after.

questions.concept: Why equipotentials are perpendicular to field lines
questions.question: Equipotential surfaces always cross field lines at right angles. Give the reason from the definition of work.
questions.solution: Moving a charge along an equipotential involves no change in potential energy, so no work is done, so the force has zero component along that path. Zero component means perpendicular: the field is normal to the surface. If field lines crossed at any other angle, work would be done along an equipotential — a contradiction.

questions.concept: Why the path does not matter
questions.question: The work done in moving a charge between two points in an electrostatic field is path-independent. Why is this the source of the idea of potential?
questions.solution: Because the electrostatic force is CONSERVATIVE — work depends only on end points, exactly as for gravity. That allows a potential energy to be defined for each point, independent of how you got there: W = q(V_A − V_B). Path independence is what makes the concept of a scalar potential possible at all; a non-conservative field would have no potential.
